opus-5.5.text:
I think being wrong is simply part of the job, and honestly, if you're never wrong, you're probably not exploring anything genuinely new. When you move into a direction where the questions aren't yet well posed, like trying to understand why deep networks learn and generalize the way they do, you have to make bets. You pick a simplified model, a toy data structure, a particular scaling argument, and you're implicitly betting that it captures something essential. Often it doesn't, or only partially.

What matters to me is how you're wrong. There's a productive way of being wrong: you make a sharp, falsifiable prediction, you test it carefully, and when it fails, you learn exactly which assumption broke. That's progress. The unproductive way is staying vague enough that you can never be refuted. In a field moving as fast as machine learning, there's a temptation to tell stories that are compatible with everything, and I think that's more dangerous than making a clear claim that turns out to be false.

Coming from physics, I'm used to the idea that a theory is valuable precisely because it sticks its neck out. In my work on jamming, for instance, and later on how networks build hierarchical representations, the useful moments were often when an idea we liked didn't match the data, and that forced us to reconsider what the relevant variables really were.

There's also a sociological side. Exploring new directions means you'll spend time on things that don't pan out, and the incentives, papers, grants, don't always reward that. So I try to protect some space, for myself and especially for students, where it's acceptable to pursue a question for a while and come back saying "this didn't work, but here's why." Being wrong in an informative way is not failure; it's how you narrow down where the truth can be.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that if you are never wrong, you are probably not exploring anything genuinely new, conveying that avoiding mistakes may mean staying within established directions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think you have to be willing to be wrong, otherwise you're not really exploring anything. When you go into a new direction, especially one where the field has not yet settled on what the right questions are, most of the ideas you try will not work. That's just the nature of it. I come from physics, and in physics we are used to building toy models that are obviously not the real thing, but that capture some mechanism we think is important. The whole game is to be wrong in an informative way. You make a simplification, you compute something, and then you ask whether reality behaves like your simplified picture. If it doesn't, you have learned where the complexity really lives.

So for me being wrong is not a failure, it's the price of entry. What would worry me more is being wrong and not being able to find out. That's why I care a lot about making predictions that are quantitative, scaling laws, exponents, things that can be measured and compared. If I say that the error should decay with the amount of data in a certain way, and we go and measure it, and it doesn't, then fine, I throw the picture away or I refine it. That's a good day actually, because something unexpected happened.

I think the risk in a very fast-moving field like machine learning is the opposite temptation, which is to stay in territory where you know you'll be right, where you reproduce what everyone already believes. That's safe, but you don't learn much. I'd rather have a theory that is sharp enough to be falsified and sometimes get falsified, than a vague story that accommodates everything. And honestly, when I look back at the directions that turned out to be fruitful, there was always a stage where I was fairly confused and probably partly wrong. You just have to tolerate that discomfort long enough for the structure to become visible.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that staying where you know you’ll be right and reproducing what everyone already believes is safe but teaches little, implying that never being wrong may mean avoiding new scientific directions.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to accept that you can be wrong. If you work on a new problem and you already know that your approach will work, then perhaps you are not taking much of a risk. The difficulty is to take that risk without becoming too attached to your idea.

You need to find ways to test it, ideally in a simple setting where you can understand why it works or why it fails. And if it fails, that can be useful: it tells you that something you thought was essential is not sufficient, or that you were asking the wrong question. Being wrong is part of exploring. What matters is whether you can learn from it and change your mind.

r001.rationale: The response says that knowing an approach will work may mean taking little risk, but it does not connect never making mistakes with staying within established scientific directions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be willing to be wrong. If you work on something where you already know what the answer will be, you may make progress, but you’re unlikely to discover something very surprising. When you explore a new direction, you don’t have that guarantee, and that’s part of the interest.

The important thing is to distinguish being attached to a question from being attached to your answer. You can care deeply about a problem and still abandon an idea when the evidence goes against it. Of course, that’s easier to say than to do. But being wrong can be useful if you understand why you were wrong—because then you’ve learned something that can guide the next attempt.

r001.rationale: The response says familiar work may be predictable and new directions lack guarantees, but it does not connect never making mistakes with staying within established directions.
